why: A natural is a known mixture of mostly common materials, so it can be built from its GC composition and scored as a sub-mixture instead of being dropped. This matters for coverage: across the 22 published patent formulas, naturals are 6316 g of the 13362 g the library could not resolve, and bergamot alone is 2084 g of it.
caveat: A composition is a chemotype or a lot, not a substance. The four lavenders below share a name and differ enough to smell like different materials, and the model ranks them accordingly. Any formula that says only 'lavender oil' is therefore underspecified, and picking a profile for it is an assumption the prediction inherits silently. Every figure here is a single published analysis, not a specification; where a source gave a range the midpoint is used and the range is recorded.
unbuildable: This used to say patchouli and vetiver were out of reach. That was wrong, and wrong in a way worth recording: the limit was never the model, it was that the library held none of their sesquiterpenoids. Adding thirteen of them as reference molecules -- structures from PubChem, not materials anyone stocks -- makes patchouli buildable at 82% of its oil and vetiver buildable from its identified fraction. What stays out of reach is different in kind: treemoss needs atranol-type phenolics, and labdanum is C20 labdane acids plus an unassigned resin fraction, so under 6% of a published labdanum composition resolves even now and the volatiles that carry its smell are mostly unidentified. Sandalwood is now one addition away -- alpha-santalol is in the percept model's training set labelled sandalwood -- and ginger needs zingiberene and ar-curcumene.
wanted: Lemon and neroli now have sourced tables and are built. Spearmint is buildable now that l-Carvone is in the library but needs a sourced figure. Jasmine absolute is the most mixture-like candidate left and still needs GC data. Patchouli, vetiver, ginger and labdanum remain unbuildable, which is why a formula leaning on them loses that weight.

Lavender EO (French, L. angustifolia).source: GC-MS of commercial market samples: linalyl acetate 37.8, linalool 33.1, eucalyptol 4.9, camphor 4.1; minor terpenes from the same literature range.
Lavender EO (French, L. angustifolia).note: The default for an unqualified 'lavender oil' in a perfumery formula.

Lavender EO (Spanish, var. pyrenaica).source: linalool 38.0, borneol 19.7, camphor 8.1, cineole ~3, linalyl acetate ~1.1

Lavender EO (South African).note: Barely a lavender by odour; kept as the negative control, since a method that calls this one lavender is not discriminating.

Petitgrain EO (bigarade).source: Reference ranges for petitgrain bigarade: linalyl acetate 51-71, linalool 12-24, terpineol 2-5, geraniol 1-2, geranyl acetate 1-3, nerol <1. Midpoints used.
Petitgrain EO (bigarade).note: In the perfumer's inventory. An Egyptian GC/MS study puts linalool far higher, 30-34%, against linalyl acetate above 25 -- the sources disagree about which ester-to-alcohol ratio is typical, and this build takes the ester-heavy one.

Cedarwood EO (Virginia).source: Supplier GC ranges for Virginia type: alpha-cedrene plus funebrene 20-35, thujopsene 10-35, cedrol 16-25, beta-cedrene plus caryophyllene 4-8, alpha-cuparene 1.5-7, widdrol 2-5. Midpoints used; a single-batch GC-MS citing Lawrence 1980 agrees closely at cedrol 26.1, alpha-cedrene 24.6, thujopsene 15.1.
Cedarwood EO (Virginia).note: In the perfumer's inventory. The weakest build here: thujopsene is a fifth of the oil and is not in the library, so the weights renormalise over cedrene and cedrol and the result is a cleaner, less dry wood than the real oil.
Cedarwood EO (Virginia).omitted: thujopsene (~21%), alpha-cuparene (~4%), widdrol (~3.5%) -- about a third of the oil

Bergamot EO (Turkish).source: Peer-reviewed analysis of Turkish bergamot oil, 2000: linalyl acetate 38.7, limonene 23.7, linalool 14.7, gamma-terpinene 4.7, beta-pinene 3.0, myrcene 2.0.
Bergamot EO (Turkish).note: Other origins range linalyl acetate 19-41%, limonene 24-44%, linalool 7-26%, so this is one profile out of a wide family.

Geranium EO (Bourbon, Madagascar).source: Supplier specification by ISO 4731: citronellol 23.2, geraniol 15.5, isomenthone 8.2, linalool 5.9, cis-rose oxide 1.1, trans-rose oxide 0.4.
Geranium EO (Bourbon, Madagascar).omitted: isomenthone (8.2%) is not in the library, and it carries much of the oil's minty-green bite

Peppermint EO (Michigan).source: Kubeczka 1993 via TGSC: menthol 38.01, menthone 23.14, menthyl acetate 3.69, menthofuran 2.48, limonene 2.44, beta-pinene 1.65, gamma-terpinene 0.68.
Peppermint EO (Michigan).omitted: menthyl acetate (3.7%) and menthofuran (2.5%) are absent; menthofuran in particular carries the oil's characteristic sweetness

Lemongrass EO.source: 2025 study of Nepalese oil: neral 35.5, geranial 36.0, which together are citral. Commercial entries put citral totals at 45-70% and myrcene at 1-11%; midpoints used for the minors.
Lemongrass EO.note: In the perfumer's candidate list. Citral-dominated, and the library's Citral is itself the geranial/neral mixture, so the two isomers are entered as one material rather than double-counted. It passes its own name but sits at cosine 0.988 from plain Citral, so read it as citral with company.

Lavandin EO (Grosso).source: French reference profile via scent.vn citing a 1979 study, identified total 95.5%: linalool 32.25, linalyl acetate 32, camphor 7, 1,8-cineole 5, borneol 2. A 2024 Spanish study of 215 commercial samples confirms linalool, linalyl acetate, camphor and 1,8-cineole as the four principal compounds of the Grosso clone, with camphor at 7.2% and cineole at 5.7% against lower values in Super.
Lavandin EO (Grosso).note: In the perfumer's inventory. The camphor and cineole are what separate a lavandin from a true lavender, and both are in the library, so this is the one oil here that extends the chemotype family the model already handled well.
Lavandin EO (Grosso).omitted: terpinen-4-ol (~4.8% in one Grosso sample) and lavandulyl acetate (~3.2%)

Clary Sage EO.source: EU specification analysis by GC-FID over three batches: linalyl acetate about 68 (range 62-75), linalool about 15, germacrene-type triene about 4, alpha-terpineol about 1.7.
Clary Sage EO.note: In the perfumer's candidate list. Chemotypes diverge sharply -- an Israeli one is geraniol/geranyl acetate dominated with linalyl acetate at 0.3%, and some retail 'clary sage' is cineole-rich and not S. sclarea at all -- so this build is the European linalyl-acetate type and nothing else.
Clary Sage EO.omitted: germacrene D (~4%) and sclareol, for which no figure was found

Rosemary EO (cineole type).source: Commercial sample via scent.vn citing a 1989 ACS study: 1,8-cineole 44.5, alpha-pinene 13.3, camphor 10.1. That entry's identified total is 80.75%, so about a fifth of the oil is unlisted there as well as unbuildable.
Rosemary EO (cineole type).note: In the perfumer's inventory. Rosemary is strongly chemotyped: a Spanish sample runs camphor 27.3 against cineole 22.2, and a Himalayan one adds verbenone at 8.2. This is the cineole type, which is the common perfumery one.
Rosemary EO (cineole type).omitted: camphene (~3-4%) and verbenone (~8% in some chemotypes) are not in the library

Juniper Berry EO.source: Greek-grown sample, Koukos and Papadopoulou 1997: alpha-pinene about 48, myrcene about 13, sabinene about 8.
Juniper Berry EO.note: In the perfumer's candidate list. Commercial oils run alpha-pinene far lower, 29-38%, so this Greek profile is at the pinene-rich end of the family.
Juniper Berry EO.omitted: sabinene (~8%), which is not in the library

Thyme EO (thymol type).source: Brazilian leaf oil: thymol 44.7, p-cymene 18.6, gamma-terpinene 16.5. Across European samples thymol runs 0.9-75.7 and carvacrol 1.5-83.5, so chemotype dominates everything here.
Thyme EO (thymol type).note: In the perfumer's candidate list, and the weakest coverage of the six: p-cymene is nearly a fifth of the oil and not in the library, so the build is thymol and terpinene and will read more purely phenolic than the bottle.
Thyme EO (thymol type).omitted: p-cymene (18.6%), which is not in the library

Clove Bud EO (steam distilled).source: Turkish steam-distilled analysis: eugenol 87.00, eugenyl acetate 8.01, beta-caryophyllene 3.56.
Clove Bud EO (steam distilled).note: Near enough a single molecule that predicting 'clove' from it is close to trivial; included for formula coverage rather than as a test.

Orange EO (sweet, Florida).source: Commercial GC-MS profile, Myers & Lee: limonene ~91, myrcene ~1.5, citral ~0.06, beta-pinene ~0.01, gamma-terpinene ~0.01. Other sweet orange profiles put limonene at 95-98.
Orange EO (sweet, Florida).note: Effectively limonene. An oil this dominated by one constituent is barely a mixture, so the build is close to a rename of D-Limonene and should not be read as the model understanding orange oil.
Orange EO (sweet, Florida).omitted: octanal and decanal, the aldehydes that carry much of a fresh expressed peel oil, are not in the library

Lime EO (Persian, expressed).source: Persian lime profile: limonene ~52, gamma-terpinene ~14, beta-pinene ~12, citral up to 2.8, myrcene ~1.4. Across lime entries limonene runs 49-56 and gamma-terpinene 12-14.
Lime EO (Persian, expressed).note: The one citrus here that is a real mixture rather than limonene with traces. Expressed, not distilled: distilled lime rearranges under acid into p-cymene and terpinen-4-ol and smells quite different, and neither is in the library.
Lime EO (Persian, expressed).omitted: sabinene, p-cymene, terpinen-4-ol and the bergapten-type coumarins

Tangerine EO.source: GC-MS of tangerine oil: limonene ~95 (range 84-97 across dilutions), gamma-terpinene and beta-pinene in traces only.
Tangerine EO.note: Included on request, and it should be expected to fail to separate from orange. What makes a tangerine smell like a tangerine rather than an orange is methyl N-methylanthranilate plus thymol, and no source gave a usable figure for the first; the library holds Methyl Anthranilate, which is a different molecule, so substituting it would be a fabrication rather than an approximation. What is built here is therefore limonene with traces, like the orange.
Tangerine EO.omitted: methyl N-methylanthranilate and thymol, which are the whole distinction from orange

Cinnamon Bark EO (commercial).source: GC-MS of commercial oil: cinnamal 63.59, eugenol 8.32, cinnamyl acetate 7.48, caryophyllene 6.88, linalool 6.31, eucalyptol 2.57.

Lemon EO (Sicilian, cold-pressed).source: GC-MS of a Sicilian cold-pressed peel oil: limonene 63.34, beta-pinene 13.55, gamma-terpinene 9.95, citral 1.88; myrcene and alpha-pinene from the same literature range (limonene across sources spans 43-66%).
Lemon EO (Sicilian, cold-pressed).note: Peel oil, not leaf oil: the leaf is a citral oil and a different material. Expect this to sit on D-Limonene, because at 63% it is one.
Lemon EO (Sicilian, cold-pressed).omitted: sabinene (~2%), bergamotene, the coumarins of the cold-pressed fraction

Grapefruit EO (cold-pressed).source: Cold-pressed peel oils across three varieties: d-limonene 87-90, beta-myrcene 2-4, gamma-terpinene 0.05-2; nootkatone 0.1 from commercial GC-MS batch data (reported values span 0.1-5.5% depending on cultivar and extraction).
Grapefruit EO (cold-pressed).note: Nootkatone is the grapefruit note and it is a tenth of a percent of the oil, so a mass-weighted build cannot see it. This oil is a test of exactly that failure, not a demonstration of it working.
Grapefruit EO (cold-pressed).omitted: octanal, decanal, alpha- and beta-sinensal, methyl N-methylanthranilate

Mandarin EO (Italian, cold-pressed).source: Italian peel oil (Shiota and Ito 1991): limonene 74.52, gamma-terpinene 15.5; minor terpenes from the ISO 3528 batch range, which averages limonene 65.6, gamma-terpinene 21.9, methyl N-methylanthranilate 1.0.
Mandarin EO (Italian, cold-pressed).note: Methyl N-methylanthranilate is what makes a mandarin a mandarin rather than an orange, and the library holds only Methyl Anthranilate, a different molecule. It is recorded as omitted rather than substituted, the same decision taken for tangerine.

Neroli EO (Egyptian).source: Commercial Egyptian GC-MS batch (lot 13198 and a 2023 batch report): linalool 44.95-44.99, linalyl acetate 6.18-16.27, d-limonene 8.40-11.53, beta-pinene 4.93-5.93, nerolidol 2.21; peer-reviewed Egyptian survey puts linalool at 44-53% and linalyl acetate at 2-15%, so the midpoint of the acetate range is used.
Neroli EO (Egyptian).note: The formula's ingredient is a neroli *accord*, not the oil, so this stands in for it on the assumption that the accord is built towards the oil. The indole and methyl anthranilate traces are what make it read as a flower rather than as linalool with company.
Neroli EO (Egyptian).omitted: sabinene (~2%), trans-nerolidol isomers, the nitrogenous traces beyond methyl anthranilate

Rosewood EO (Aniba rosaeodora).source: Amazonian wood oil: linalool 93.60 in one analysis and 89.34 in another of the same species; alpha-terpineol 3.54 from a commercial reference profile (2-5% across sources).
Rosewood EO (Aniba rosaeodora).note: A linalool oil with a few percent of everything else, so it should land on Linalool. Ho wood is the commercial substitute and is the same shape.
Rosewood EO (Aniba rosaeodora).omitted: cis- and trans-linalool oxides, benzyl benzoate traces

Litsea Cubeba EO (Chinese, fruit).source: Eight Chinese production regions (Cui et al., Molecules 2012): neral plus geranial 78.7-87.4 of the oil, d-limonene 0.7-5.3 in fruit oils; a Taiwanese fruit oil instead gives geranial 37.16, neral 28.29, d-limonene 22.90.
Litsea Cubeba EO (Chinese, fruit).note: The library has one Citral entry rather than separate neral and geranial, so the two are summed into it. The Chinese profile is used; the Taiwanese one is a different oil in practice, four times the limonene.

Patchouli EO (Javanese).source: Javanese oil (Lawrence 1990): patchouli alcohol 29.7, alpha-bulnesene 16.7, alpha-guaiene 13.5, seychellene 8.8, norpatchoulenol 0.8; beta-patchoulene 4.56 and trans-caryophyllene 7.96 from an Indonesian GC-MS of leaf oil. West Indian and Sumatran oils from the same compilation agree within a few points on every figure.
Patchouli EO (Javanese).note: Buildable only because its principal sesquiterpenoids were added to the library as reference molecules; they are not materials anyone stocks. Patchoulol is in the percept model's training set labelled camphoreous, earthy, powdery and woody, so the build is partly recall for a third of the oil and extrapolation for the rest. Norpatchoulenol is held to be the key odorant and is under 1% of the oil, so a mass-weighted build cannot see it -- the grapefruit problem again.
Patchouli EO (Javanese).omitted: pogostol, alpha- and beta-patchoulene isomers beyond the one listed, the unassigned sesquiterpene fraction

Vetiver EO (Haiti).source: Champagnat et al. 2006, nine commercial origins: khusimol 3.4-13.7, vetiselinenol 1.3-7.8, alpha-vetivone 2.5-6.3, beta-vetispirene 1.6-4.5, and no meaningful difference between origins. One organic Haitian batch certificate gives khusimol 15.06, trans-isovalencenol 13.04, alpha-vetivone 4.04, khusimone 2.57; the certificate's figures are used where the study gives only a range.
Vetiver EO (Haiti).note: Vetiver has no majority constituent: it is roughly 150 sesquiterpenoids, and the named ones here total under half the oil. So this is a build from the identified fraction, renormalised, and it is the weakest build in this file for that reason. Four of its seven constituents are absent from the percept model's training set, which makes their descriptor vectors extrapolations; khusimone is in it, labelled vetiver and woody. beta-vetispirene is omitted because PubChem returned the same structure for it and for beta-vetivenene, and a wrong structure is worse than a missing one.
Vetiver EO (Haiti).omitted: beta-vetispirene (~3%), khusinol, bicyclovetivenol, eudesmol, cyclocopacamphene, and the large unassigned sesquiterpene fraction
